The proposed combination of token-level information gain, method-level semantic alignment, and length control is technically interesting. The paper also includes useful component ablations and training-dynamics plots rather than reporting only a final aggregate result.

The presentation is generally clear, and the appendices document dataset construction, baseline adaptations, reward thresholds, hyperparameters, evaluation prompts, and qualitative examples in substantial detail.
Including blinded judgments from three PhD researchers is a positive attempt to validate the automated evaluation rather than relying exclusively on an LLM judge.
weaknesses: The central evidence does not establish genuinely novel scientific ideation. Both reward components explicitly favor reconstruction of the held-out ground-truth method: CSG directly rewards embedding similarity to that method, while EAIG rewards reasoning that makes its high-entropy tokens predictable. A reasoning trace can therefore repeat or encode ground-truth technical content; the format check only excludes headers and does not test such leakage. This is fundamentally at odds with claims of moving beyond imitation or learning authentic discovery.

Evaluation validity is the decisive concern. Nearly all reported conclusions rely on Gemini-2.5-Pro scores, yet the judge may have encountered the ICLR 2024–2025 papers during training or retrieve the target paper itself. The paper does not report judge decontamination, target-paper filtering, uncertainty, or significance tests. Ground-truth papers receiving high novelty scores makes it especially unclear what comparison set the judge is using.

The human study is too small and its analysis insufficient to validate the judge. It contains only 15 examples from each of four systems, omits several evaluated baselines, and reports neither inter-annotator agreement nor uncertainty. Pearson correlation pooled across systems can be inflated by between-system score differences and does not demonstrate reliable within-context ranking; the assertion that systematic LLM over-scoring does not affect rankings is unsupported.

The baseline comparisons are not controlled. Agentic systems are substantially modified: stages are bypassed, local models are replaced, VirSci receives fewer discussion rounds, and outputs are expanded by GPT-4o. AI-Scientist-V2 uses only one generation despite its tree-search motivation. There is also no compute-matched base-model prompting baseline. Consequently, the results do not support the broad conclusion that internalized reasoning is superior to external scaffolding.

The claimed theoretical account of GRPO length bias is not rigorous. Within-group standardized advantages necessarily sum to zero, so the stated explanation that low-variance strategies yield consistently positive advantages does not follow, and the proposed Sharpe-ratio objective is asserted rather than derived. The empirical narrative is also contradictory: the main text describes EAIG-only training as causing length explosion, whereas Appendix F and Table 9 describe higher EAIG weight as causing the shortest-chain collapse.

Hyperparameters appear to be selected using the same evaluation set on which final performance is reported; no development set is described. Ablations are evaluated at step 100 while the main model is reported at step 400, and the assertion that early trends match convergence is not demonstrated. Results from only one apparent training run, without seed variance, further weaken the 0.20-point RL-over-SFT improvement.

The qualitative MoRI example itself contains unsupported or technically questionable details, including a claim of reduced computation and a purported DPO procedure without clearly defined preference pairs. This conflicts with the automated judge's assessment of high technical rigor and illustrates why real expert review or downstream implementation experiments are necessary.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: code is only promised, the processed dataset and exact split identifiers are unavailable, and important extraction/reconstruction prompts and decontamination procedures are missing. Base, teacher, embedding, and judge models may all have prior exposure to the source papers. A sound Findings case requires a leakage-controlled evaluation, stronger human validation, uncertainty across runs, and fairer baselines.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and difficult NLP problem: generating technically substantive scientific ideas rather than merely fluent proposals.

The motivation-to-reasoning-to-method formulation is clearly presented, and the manuscript provides concrete reward definitions, training hyperparameters, prompts, ablations, and qualitative examples.
The authors compare against commercial models, supervised fine-tuning, and several agentic systems, and they make a useful attempt to validate automated evaluation with blinded human judgments.
The ablations expose meaningful optimization behavior, including instability when the information-gain reward is used alone, rather than reporting only the best configuration.
weaknesses: The central experiment is closer to reconstructing held-out papers than open-ended scientific ideation. Both rewards explicitly use the ground-truth methodology: EAIG rewards reasoning that makes its tokens predictable, while CSG rewards semantic similarity to it. These objectives directly encourage recovery of the known solution, so performance does not establish an ability to devise novel methods. The format check does not prevent the reasoning trace from leaking substantive ground-truth method content.

EAIG is not the claimed causal measure of reasoning contribution. It compares the current policy conditioned on the trace against the SFT policy without the trace, thereby confounding the effect of the trace with changes to model parameters. A valid attribution comparison would at least evaluate the same fixed model with and without the trace. The assumption that high predictive entropy identifies innovative technical content is also asserted rather than validated.

The evidence does not support claims that MoRI internalizes robust scientific reasoning or transcends imitation. Training traces are retrospective rationalizations rewritten with access to the target method, and longer outputs or higher target-likelihood rewards do not demonstrate faithful reasoning. No intervention, trace-faithfulness test, or downstream implementation experiment is provided.

The length-bias account is technically unconvincing: within-group advantage normalization is presented as implicit Sharpe-ratio optimization without a justified policy-gradient derivation. The manuscript is also internally contradictory: the main text describes EAIG-only training as producing length explosion, whereas Appendix F says 100% EAIG produces the shortest traces and that increasing EAIG accelerates length collapse.

Almost all headline results come from one Gemini-based judge. The 60-item human study is too limited to validate the full ranking: it excludes Claude, Full-SFT, ResearchAgent, and VirSci; reports no inter-annotator agreement; and pools deliberately stratified sources when computing Pearson correlation, which can inflate correlation through between-system differences. There are no confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or human evidence for MoRI's claimed advantage over its strongest baselines.

The test and model-selection protocol is insufficiently specified. The meaning of 83 papers published in 'late 2025' within an ICLR 2024-2025 collection is unclear, contamination from base-model pretraining is not investigated, and it is not stated whether reward weights, entropy thresholds, length settings, and the selected 400-step checkpoint were tuned on the same holdout used for reporting. Retrieval-based evaluation introduces another possible route to the target papers.

Baseline comparisons are difficult to interpret because the authors substantially modify the agentic systems: stages are bypassed, VirSci uses different models and fewer rounds, and short outputs are expanded by an additional LLM. AI-Scientist-V2's reported Claude variant uses Claude Haiku, while comparison language suggests a stronger agentic baseline. These changes may disadvantage the baselines and do not isolate internal reasoning from compute, model, or output-expansion effects.

Important controls are missing, especially generated versus oracle motivation at training and inference, the benefit of motivation conditioning over matched direct generation, target-free rewards, and comparisons under equal data and inference-compute budgets. The Full-SFT data accounting is also ambiguous because the RL subset reportedly yields only about 2,000 valid examples while Full-SFT uses the union of 8,000 samples.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate. Code is only promised; dataset identifiers, extraction and posterior-rewriting prompts, SFT settings, random seeds, hardware and cost, exact filtering counts, numerical anchor length, and full retrieval details are absent. The data description is inconsistent about whether outputs contain cleaned method sections or only abstracted ideas without methodological details.

Feasibility and scientific validity are judged from proposal prose rather than implementation. The qualitative MoRI example itself contains underspecified or questionable training targets and DPO claims, illustrating why polished methodological detail is not evidence that an idea works. Overall, repairing the evaluation target, theoretical justification, leakage controls, and human validation requires substantial reconstruction beyond a routine next-cycle revision.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem—scientific ideation—and offers a coherent motivation-to-method formulation rather than another purely agentic workflow.
MoRI combines a technically interesting entropy-filtered information-gain signal with semantic alignment, and the paper provides clear equations, training-dynamics analyses, and component ablations.
The evaluation covers commercial models, supervised training, and several scientific-ideation agents. The human study provides useful, though incomplete, corroboration of the automated evaluation.
The manuscript is well organized and unusually detailed about baseline adaptations, judge prompts, reward shaping, and RL hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The evidence does not fully substantiate the central claim that MoRI internalizes scientific reasoning. EAIG and CSG explicitly reward agreement with ground-truth methods, while the reported evaluation measures plausibility of generated proposals rather than successful scientific discovery or transferable reasoning.

EAIG is described as the causal contribution of reasoning, but it compares different models under different conditioning: log pi_theta(y*|x,m,z) versus log pi_SFT(y*|x,m). The resulting gain conflates the presence of z with policy-parameter changes and therefore does not isolate reasoning's contribution.

The theoretical account of GRPO as implicitly maximizing a Sharpe-ratio-like objective is not rigorously derived. Within-group normalized advantages have zero mean, and the argument that low-variance strategies accumulate consistently positive advantages does not follow as written.

The decisive comparison against Full-SFT is supported only by the Gemini judge. Human evaluation excludes Full-SFT and Claude, pools systems of widely separated quality when computing correlation, reports no inter-annotator agreement or pairwise significance, and therefore does not establish that the relatively small RL gain is perceptible to experts.

Main results lack uncertainty estimates, statistical tests, multiple training seeds, and sensitivity analysis for several calibrated reward thresholds. Selecting the reported configuration and checkpoint using the same automatic judge raises additional model-selection concerns.

Leakage and contamination controls are insufficiently demonstrated. Test contexts are extracted from ICLR papers whose submissions may predate the stated publication split, pretrained models may have encountered them, and lexical filtering does not establish that retrieval systems or the evaluation judge cannot recover the target paper.

Several agentic baselines are materially altered: stages are removed, models and discussion counts are changed, and outputs are expanded by another LLM. These adaptations complicate claims that internalized reasoning outperforms the original agentic approaches.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code is only promised, extraction and posterior-reconstruction prompts are absent, SFT and inference details are incomplete, hardware and compute costs are unreported, and dynamic anchor-length selection is underspecified.

The qualitative example contains substantial technical ambiguity—for example, it presents SFT and DPO as alternative training mechanisms without a fully specified executable algorithm—illustrating the gap between method-like detail and demonstrated feasibility.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem and presents a clear motivation-conditioned formulation, a concrete GRPO training pipeline, and two complementary reference-based reward components.

The experimental section is unusually extensive: it includes commercial, agentic, and supervised baselines; in-domain and cross-venue test sets; reward and conditioning ablations; training-dynamics analyses; confidence intervals; and some human evaluation.

MoRI improves substantially over the matched Full-SFT baseline, providing evidence that the RL stage contributes beyond additional supervised training. The paper is generally clear, well organized, and relevant to ACL.
weaknesses: The central claim is stronger than the evidence permits. Training and testing ask the model to reconstruct methodologies associated with existing papers from extracted topics, backgrounds, and references. Both rewards explicitly favor agreement with the one ground-truth method. This demonstrates reference-directed method reconstruction, not necessarily novel scientific ideation or 'authentic scientific discovery.'

The rewards admit important shortcuts. EAIG rewards reasoning that increases the current policy's likelihood of the reference method, so method-like content can leak into the reasoning without constituting valid deduction; excluding markdown headers does not prevent semantic leakage. CSG is principally similarity to the reference method, while its subtracted context baseline is constant across rollouts for a prompt and only affects GRPO through the nonlinear reward bins. Neither objective directly verifies scientific correctness, novelty, or causal reasoning.

The evaluation depends primarily on a Gemini judge. Its reported correlation is computed over a deliberately stratified mixture containing clearly different-quality sources, which can inflate pooled correlation and does not establish sensitivity to the smaller differences among competitive systems. The human comparison omits Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Full-SFT—the two most important baselines—and MoRI's automated advantage over Claude is statistically nonsignificant.

Potential contamination and task leakage are insufficiently controlled. Public 2024–2025 papers, their topics, reference lists, and extracted background text can identify the target work or trigger memorized content in foundation models and API judges. Removing titles and applying an 80% lexical-overlap retrieval filter is not a convincing contamination audit, and the assertion that examples cannot be reverse-identified is implausible.

Model and hyperparameter selection are not methodologically separated from evaluation: no validation split is described, yet reward weights, entropy threshold, and a 400-step checkpoint are called optimal, while ablations are reported at a selected 100-step checkpoint. This creates a serious risk of test-set tuning. Results also appear to come from a single training run, with no seed-level uncertainty.

Several interpretations are not established by the measurements. Longer generated chains are treated as deeper reasoning, and cherry-picked traces are used to infer internalized cognitive behaviors; neither rules out verbosity or post-hoc rationalization. The entropy analysis relies on a very broad heuristic that labels essentially alphabetic tokens of length at least three as technical terms and lacks random-mask or other informative-token baselines.

Baseline comparability is weakened by substantial adaptations: stages are removed, models and round counts are changed, and outputs are expanded by additional LLM calls. These comparisons no longer cleanly isolate internal reasoning from external scaffolding.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the stated code release: exact paper identifiers and temporal cutoff, extraction and reconstruction prompts, SFT hyperparameters, numerical anchor length, hardware/compute, random seeds, API/retrieval snapshots, generated outputs, and judge annotations are not fully specified. A credible revision needs contamination-resistant held-out tasks, validation-based model selection, multiple RL seeds, paired human evaluation against the strongest baselines, and an analysis separating novel ideation from recovery of the source paper's method.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem and presents a clear motivation-conditioned formulation of scientific idea generation.
The proposed composite reward is technically interesting: EAIG targets difficult tokens in reference methodologies, while CSG measures movement toward the reference solution in embedding space.

The empirical section is broader than average, including two test venues, several commercial and agentic baselines, component ablations, training-dynamics analyses, bootstrap intervals, and limited human evaluation.
The presentation is generally clear, and the appendices provide useful details about baseline adaptation, reward shaping, prompts, and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The evidence does not establish the central claim that MoRI internalizes scientific reasoning. Both rewards explicitly favor reconstruction of a known paper's methodology, and the qualitative reasoning traces are selected post hoc. Improved reference reconstruction or verbosity is not evidence of transferable scientific reasoning or authentic discovery.

EAIG is not a valid measure of the claimed causal contribution of reasoning: its likelihood difference compares the evolving RL policy conditioned on z against a different SFT model without z. It therefore conflates the effect of the reasoning trace with model-parameter changes. A same-model intervention with and without z, plus controls for target leakage, would be needed.

The evaluation is too dependent on a single Gemini judge. The reported human–LLM correlation is pooled across systems with markedly different average quality, which can inflate correlation through between-system differences. Human preference or quality comparisons between MoRI and its strongest baselines, with uncertainty and significance testing, are not reported. MoRI is not significantly better than Claude-3.5-Sonnet even under the automated judge, contradicting the broad claim of consistent superiority over strong commercial models.

Potential leakage and reconstruction bias are insufficiently controlled. Contexts and motivations are extracted from complete papers, so they may encode method-specific information. The retrieval-augmented evaluator is not stated to exclude the target paper. Temporal splits alone do not address either issue or possible pretraining exposure. Controlled leakage audits and evaluation on researcher-authored problem statements are needed.

Length anchoring directly rewards longer reasoning up to an SFT-derived threshold, while generated chains reach roughly 8,000–12,000 characters. The paper then treats increased length as evidence of deeper reasoning, without length-matched baselines or controls for known verbosity biases in LLM judges. The accompanying claim that GRPO approximately maximizes a Sharpe ratio and inherently favors low-variance short strategies is not rigorously derived from group-normalized advantages.

Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled. Several agentic systems are substantially modified, some stages are removed, models are substituted, and outputs are expanded by an additional LLM. Some agentic results are missing on the OOD set, and compute, retrieval access, output length, and sampling budgets are not matched. These results cannot cleanly support the claim that internalized reasoning is superior to external scaffolding.

Reward weights, entropy thresholds, and length mechanisms appear selected using evaluation trends, but no independent development set or model-selection protocol is specified. Ablations are reported at step 100 while the main result uses step 400, and seed-to-seed variation is absent, leaving uncertainty about RL stability and selection bias.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: exact train/test paper identifiers, extraction and posterior-reconstruction prompts, SFT hyperparameters, random seeds, hardware and compute costs, checkpoint-selection rules, retrieval settings, and complete human-annotation instructions are missing. The stated code availability alone does not resolve these omissions.

The work is relevant and potentially salvageable, but validating the main claims requires substantial new evaluation and corrected causal analysis rather than minor exposition changes. A revised submission could reasonably be prepared for a future cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem and presents a coherent motivation-to-reasoning-to-method formulation rather than relying solely on inference-time agent scaffolding.
The composite reward is technically interesting: EAIG targets difficult reference-method content, while CSG discourages context restatement and promotes solution-level alignment.

The experimental section is unusually extensive, including a strong Full-SFT baseline, reward-component and entropy-mask ablations, training-dynamics analyses, an out-of-domain NeurIPS test set, confidence intervals, and some human validation of the automated evaluator.
Results consistently favor MoRI over Full-SFT and most evaluated agentic systems, suggesting that the proposed training procedure provides a real benefit under the paper's evaluation protocol.
The manuscript is clear and well organized, and the appendices document many implementation choices, evaluation prompts, baseline adaptations, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central claim that MoRI produces genuinely better scientific ideas is not established robustly enough. Almost all reported comparisons depend on one Gemini judge, while the human study is small, covers only four sources, and primarily validates correlation rather than directly testing the key system-level superiority claims. Correlation across a deliberately broad quality range does not ensure reliable discrimination among the strongest systems.

No development split or model-selection protocol is described. The reward weights, entropy threshold, length anchoring, and 400-step checkpoint are presented as optimal based on reported evaluation results, creating a serious risk that the test sets were used for hyperparameter and checkpoint selection. This makes the final performance estimates potentially optimistic.

Leakage and memorization remain insufficiently controlled. Test contexts derived from published papers include distinctive topics and reference snippets that may identify the hidden paper to pretrained models. Removing titles and filtering retrieval results does not address model pretraining contamination or semantic retrieval of the target work, especially for 2025 papers.

Baseline fairness is uncertain because several agentic systems are substantially modified: stages are bypassed, model backbones are substituted, discussion rounds are reduced, and outputs are expanded by an additional model. Generation-length constraints also differ from MoRI's prompt. Consequently, the evidence does not cleanly support the broad claim that internalized reasoning is superior to external scaffolding.

EAIG is described as measuring the causal contribution of reasoning, but it only measures a conditional likelihood difference. It can reward reasoning that inserts reference-predictive terminology without representing a valid inferential process. Likewise, CSG explicitly optimizes similarity to the known method, so the method may favor reconstruction of canonical solutions rather than genuinely open-ended ideation.

The claimed internalization of scientific reasoning is supported mainly by longer traces, correlated proxy rewards, and selected qualitative excerpts. These observations cannot distinguish improved reasoning from verbosity, stylistic imitation, or reward optimization; no intervention, faithfulness test, or outcome-based implementation experiment is provided.

The theoretical account of GRPO's supposed variance aversion is not rigorous: the transition from group-normalized advantages to an implicit Sharpe-ratio objective is not derived and is generally unjustified. This weakens the mechanistic explanation offered for length collapse.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive appendix: data-extraction and posterior-reconstruction prompts, SFT hyperparameters, random seeds, compute configuration, exact anchor length, checkpoint-selection procedure, and several retrieval details are absent. Overall, the work is promising and close to Findings, but the evaluation-selection and leakage concerns prevent a sound positive recommendation in its current form.
